photon-jets using a Transformer architecture, which represents the state-of-the-art for
modeling high-dimensional, unordered input spaces [39]. Originally developed for natu-

and higher-order interactions between input tokens. Unlike convolutional or recurrent ar-
chitectures, they naturally accommodate variable-sized inputs and can be designed to be
permutation-invariant, making them well-suited for particle physics applications involv-
ing unordered detector hits or energy deposits. Transformers have demonstrated strong
performance across a wide range of domains in high energy physics, such as jet flavor
tagging in ATLAS [40, 41]. By explicitly modeling correlations between calorimeter cells
while accommodating a variable detector geometry, these architectures provide a flexible
framework for learning the detailed shower substructure associated with highly collimated
photon decays.

Selection Mechanism.
First, we identify a key limitation of prior models: the ability to efficiently select data in an

Hardware-aware Algorithm.
This simple change poses a technical challenge for the computation of the model; in

We simplify prior deep sequence model architectures by combining the design of prior SSM architectures

architecture design (Mamba) incorporating selective state spaces.

suitable as the backbone of general foundation models operating on sequences. (i) High quality: selectivity brings strong

We motivate our selection mechanism using intuition from synthetic tasks (Section 3.1), then explain how to incorporate
this mechanism into state space models (Section 3.2). The resulting time-varying SSMs cannot use convolutions, presenting
a technical challenge of how to compute them efficiently. We overcome this with a hardware-aware algorithm that exploits
the memory hierarchy on modern hardware (Section 3.3). We then describe a simple SSM architecture without attention or
even MLP blocks (Section 3.4). Finally, we discuss some additional properties of selection mechanisms (Section 3.5).


3.1
Motivation: Selection as a Means of Compression


We argue that a fundamental problem of sequence modeling is compressing context into a smaller state. In fact, we can
view the tradeoffs of popular sequence models from this point of view. For example, attention is both effective and
inefficient because it explicitly does not compress context at all. This can be seen from the fact that autoregressive inference
requires explicitly storing the entire context (i.e. the KV cache), which directly causes the slow linear-time inference and
quadratic-time training of Transformers. On the other hand, recurrent models are efficient because they have a finite state,
implying constant-time inference and linear-time training. However, their effectiveness is limited by how well this state
has compressed the context.


To understand this principle, we focus on two running examples of synthetic tasks (Figure 2).


• The Selective Copying task modifies the popular Copying task (Arjovsky, Shah, and Bengio 2016) by varying the
position of the tokens to memorize. It requires content-aware reasoning to be able to memorize the relevant tokens
(colored) and filter out the irrelevant ones (white).


• The Induction Heads task is a well-known mechanism hypothesized to explain the majority of in-context learning
abilities of LLMs (Olsson et al. 2022). It requires context-aware reasoning to know when to produce the correct output in
the appropriate context (black).


These tasks reveal the failure mode of LTI models. From the recurrent view, their constant dynamics (e.g. the (𝑨, 𝑩)
transitions in (2)) cannot let them select the correct information from their context, or affect the hidden state passed
along the sequence in an input-dependent way. From the convolutional view, it is known that global convolutions can
solve the vanilla Copying task (Romero et al. 2021) because it only requires time-awareness, but that they have difficulty
with the Selective Copying task because of lack of content-awareness (Figure 2). More concretely, the spacing between
inputs-to-outputs is varying and cannot be modeled by static convolution kernels.


In summary, the efficiency vs. effectiveness tradeoff of sequence models is characterized by how well they compress
their state: efficient models must have a small state, while effective models must have a state that contains all necessary

Motivation: Selection as a Means of Compression


We argue that a fundamental problem of sequence modeling is compressing context into a smaller state. In fact, we can
view the tradeoffs of popular sequence models from this point of view. For example, attention is both effective and
inefficient because it explicitly does not compress context at all. This can be seen from the fact that autoregressive inference
requires explicitly storing the entire context (i.e. the KV cache), which directly causes the slow linear-time inference and
quadratic-time training of Transformers. On the other hand, recurrent models are efficient because they have a finite state,
implying constant-time inference and linear-time training. However, their effectiveness is limited by how well this state
has compressed the context.

• The Selective Copying task modifies the popular Copying task (Arjovsky, Shah, and Bengio 2016) by varying the
position of the tokens to memorize. It requires content-aware reasoning to be able to memorize the relevant tokens
(colored) and filter out the irrelevant ones (white).

the appropriate context (black).

along the sequence in an input-dependent way. From the convolutional view, it is known that global convolutions can

information from the context. In turn, we propose that a fundamental principle for building sequence models is selectivity:
or the context-aware ability to focus on or filter out inputs into a sequential state. In particular, a selection mechanism
controls how information propagates or interacts along the sequence dimension (see Section 3.5 for more discussion).

## Selective State Space Models

**Where the idea sits.** State space models (SSMs), specifically the structured S4 family, are a class of deep-learning sequence models related to RNNs, CNNs, and classical state-space systems. An S4 model is defined by four parameters (Δ, **A**, **B**, **C**) that map an input sequence to an output through a latent state **h**, via a continuous system that is discretized and then run either as a linear recurrence or a global convolution (`2312.00752.pdf`, p. 3). These models did well on continuous-signal domains (audio, vision) but were **less effective at discrete, information-dense data such as text** (p. 2).

**The core proposal.** The paper proposes "a new class of **selective state space models**, that improves on prior work on several axes to achieve the modeling power of Transformers while scaling linearly in sequence length" (p. 2). The identified weakness of prior SSMs is their **inability to perform content-based reasoning** — because they are Linear Time-Invariant (LTI), the parameters (Δ, **A**, **B**, **C**) are fixed for all timesteps (p. 3), so the model cannot focus on or ignore particular inputs based on their content.

**The mechanism (selection).** The fix is to **make the SSM parameters functions of the input**, so the model can selectively propagate or forget information along the sequence depending on the current token (p. 1–2). Concretely, the parameters Δ, **B**, and **C** become input-dependent projections — `s_B(x)=Linear_N(x)`, `s_C(x)=Linear_N(x)`, `s_Δ(x)=Broadcast_D(Linear_1(x))` with `τ_Δ=softplus` — giving them a length dimension L and turning the model from **time-invariant into time-varying** (p. 5). This is shown as the difference between Algorithm 1 (S4) and Algorithm 2 (SSM + Selection, called **S6**), where **B**, **C**, and Δ pick up (B, L, …) shapes (p. 6).

**Why selection matters (motivation).** Sequence modeling is framed as compressing context into a smaller state, a tradeoff between efficiency and effectiveness: attention doesn't compress at all (effective but slow, needs a KV cache), while recurrent models have a finite state (efficient but limited by how well the state compresses context) (p. 5). Two synthetic tasks expose the failure mode of LTI models: **Selective Copying** (varying token spacing, needs content-awareness to memorize relevant tokens and filter irrelevant ones) and **Induction Heads** (context-aware associative recall) — LTI models with constant dynamics cannot select the correct information in an input-dependent way (p. 5, Figure 2 on p. 6). The paper's guiding principle is **selectivity**: the context-aware ability to focus on or filter inputs into a sequential state.

**The cost and the fix (hardware-aware algorithm).** Making the model input-dependent **breaks the equivalence to convolutions**, so the efficient convolutional training mode is lost and the model must run as a recurrence/scan (p. 5–6). To keep this efficient, the authors use a **hardware-aware algorithm**: it computes the model recurrently with a scan, and crucially **does not materialize the expanded state** (shape B, L, D, N) in slow GPU memory — it keeps the state in the faster levels of the GPU memory hierarchy (SRAM vs HBM), avoiding costly IO. The result is faster than prior methods — linear scaling in sequence length (vs pseudo-linear for convolution-based SSMs) and **up to 3× faster on A100 GPUs** (p. 2–3, Figure 1 on p. 3).

**The architecture (Mamba).** These selective SSMs are integrated into a **simplified, homogeneous architecture without attention or MLP blocks**, called **Mamba** (p. 2). Mamba is fully recurrent, with three key properties: (i) **high quality** — selectivity yields strong performance on dense modalities like language and genomics; (ii) **fast training and inference** — linear-time training and constant-time-per-step autoregressive inference with no cache; (iii) **long context** — improvements on real data up to sequence length 1M (p. 2).

**Empirical results (all p. 2).** Mamba's abstract/intro claims:
- **Synthetics** — solves copying and induction-head tasks and extrapolates beyond 1M tokens.
- **Audio & genomics** — outperforms SaShiMi, Hyena, and Transformers, improving with longer context.
- **Language modeling** — the first linear-time model to reach Transformer-quality performance; **5× higher generation throughput** than comparable Transformers, and **Mamba-3B matches Transformers twice its size** (e.g., exceeding Pythia-7B on common-sense reasoning) (also stated in the abstract, p. 1).
